stories.headline: Vatican City: Pope says Mass for Gemelli staff; Sunday Angelus confirmed
stories.body: On his fourth day in hospital, Pope Leo XIV celebrated noon Mass in the room set up on Gemelli’s 10th floor, gave Communion to off-duty doctors, nurses, and Vatican gendarmes, and thanked them in his homily for caring for patients “in their frailty” — and for him. The Vatican released the first photos since Tuesday’s lung surgery: the Pope standing at a small altar in green vestments. Friday’s bulletin from Dr. Luigi Carbone and Prof. Stefano Margaritora says blood tests and a chest X-ray confirm “steady improvement,” and that he carries out daily activities with complete autonomy. The Press Office says Sunday’s Angelus “will take place,” though not yet whether from the hospital or the Vatican; discharge is still expected around Tuesday, Oct. 20.
stories.why: First pictures and a public prayer on Sunday are the clearest signs yet that the recovery is on track.

stories.headline: Vatican City: Tagle and Reina visit; Parolin clarifies “readjusting the pontificate”
stories.body: Friday afternoon the Pope received Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, pro-prefect of the Dicastery for Evangelization and Dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldo Reina, his vicar general for the Diocese of Rome. Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin said his Thursday remark about “readjusting the pontificate” referred only to travel — “at least with regard to this next trip” to Latin America — not to reshaping the Pope’s duties; he added he has not yet seen the Pope in hospital. Thursday night Parolin opened the new building of Iraq’s embassy to the Holy See, 60 years after relations began, calling diplomacy the “only genuine alternative” to violence.

stories.headline: Africa: Ethiopia installs Tigray caretaker government as Tigrayan forces counterattack
stories.body: Addis Ababa suspended Tigray’s interim administration Friday and appointed a caretaker government after declaring the TPLF defeated, promising elections within six months; its five leaders come from adviser Getachew Reda’s Simret party and the Tigray Peace Forces. Yet Tigrayan forces claim a counteroffensive in central Tigray, and the conflict monitor ACLED corroborates that they retook Abiy Addi and Werkamba on Oct. 14, with drone-heavy fighting around Kola Tembien. Ethiopia showed foreign military attachés weapons it says came through Eritrea, including an Iranian-made Mohajer-6 drone; Eritrea’s foreign minister calls Ethiopia’s campaign an unjustified invasion. Critical Threats analysts read the display as groundwork to justify strikes inside Eritrea on self-defense grounds, while the U.S., EU, U.K., and Canada urge restraint; in Amhara, Fano rebels keep taking rural towns in South Wollo and North Shewa.

stories.headline: Africa: Kabila takes over Congo’s rebellion; Ebola money questioned
stories.body: Former president Joseph Kabila, who ruled Congo from 2001 to 2019, now heads the Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 alliance, renamed the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN); M23’s Sultani Makenga stays as military chief. Kabila was sentenced to death in absentia for treason a year ago and is under U.S. sanctions; the FRN says it keeps all its Doha peace commitments. On Ebola (Bundibugyo strain), Europe’s CDC counts 9,277 confirmed cases and 4,478 deaths as of Oct. 15, Ituri hardest hit, and 10 schoolchildren in Ituri have died since classes resumed. Africa CDC says donors gave about $962 million to aid groups, but only $228 million has been reported to the government — over $700 million unaccounted for, though chief Jean Kaseya says it is “too early to speak of embezzlement.”

She urged both sides to stop using drones or at least strictly regulate them, and noted both have set up committees on prisoner releases. UN figures: 20 million people face acute hunger, 200,000 at catastrophe levels, and a drone strike near the Ethiopian border killed 41 displaced people Oct. 10. The Sudan Consultative Group meets in Geneva next week, as the anniversary of El Fasher’s fall approaches; this morning’s thread continues, with Burhan’s letter to Trump while the army still rejects the 90-day truce plan.

stories.headline: Ukraine, deeper: civilian toll up 85%; Ukraine gains near Lyman
stories.body: UN monitors verified 328 civilians killed and 2,105 injured in September, 85% more than a year earlier, and call the first two weeks of October “among the deadliest periods for civilians in years”; strikes on Oct. 13–14 hit Kyiv’s three main power stations and left 600,000 people in the capital without power. On the ground, Ukraine’s Third Army Corps says Operation Vivaldi has retaken 275 square kilometers and 16 settlements in Donetsk since August, and ISW counts Russian attacks toward Sloviansk falling from about 14 a day in August to three in October. Winter is the worry: 1.45 million returnees live in frontline districts, the IAEA warns Zaporizhzhia’s backup diesel is running low, and Caritas, whose Odesa center was badly damaged by a drone last weekend minutes after clients left, is preparing heating tents and soup kitchens.
stories.why: The war is now being fought over the power grid as much as the front line, and winter decides who suffers most.

beats.headline: Vance’s fraud pledge spreads; peptide plan’s fine print; tax relief recap.

stories.headline: War on fraud: Vance pledge gathers signers; results are self-reported
stories.body: Promise: Trump promised to root out waste, fraud, and abuse in federal programs. What was done: Vice President Vance, who heads the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, asked officials at every level to sign a pledge to stop fraud “before the money goes out,” keep benefits for eligible Americans, and prosecute fraudsters; the White House lists Cabinet members, more than a dozen governors, state attorneys general, and dozens of members of Congress. Impact claimed: Labor says it has uncovered $22 billion in labor fraud, Education says it has prevented more than $2 billion in student-aid fraud, and the FBI cites six “Most Wanted” fraud arrests tied to over $2 billion. Room for disagreement: a pledge is a statement of intent, not a law; the figures are the agencies’ own, not independently audited; and every elected signer listed is a Republican — Rep. Rudy Yakym asked why no Democrat has signed. In progress.

sources.name: White House: Coalition in the war on fraud

stories.headline: MAHA peptides, deeper: advisers overruled staff; telehealth firms wait
stories.body: Promise: Kennedy said the FDA’s “war” on peptides would end. What was done: HHS sent the White House an “interim access policy” that would use enforcement discretion, telling compounding pharmacies they won’t be targeted for making peptides like BPC-157; formally listing them as safe to compound would take rulemaking that could last years. In July a panel of outside advisers, chosen by HHS and including people who work in the peptide field, recommended lifting limits on six of seven peptides, against the conclusion of FDA staff scientists. Impact: Hims & Hers and Noom plan to sell peptides if access eases, in a market analysts put at $2 billion to $3 billion; supporters call it medical freedom, and the FDA has listed risks including contamination, allergic reactions, and tumor growth. Not yet in effect.

stories.headline: No tax on tips and overtime: partly kept, capped through 2028
stories.body: Promise: Trump campaigned on ending federal taxes on tips and overtime. What was done: The July 2025 tax law created deductions, not a full repeal: up to $25,000 of tips, plus the extra “half” of time-and-a-half overtime, through 2028, with payroll taxes still owed. Treasury’s first-season data: more than 7.5 million filers claimed the tips deduction (average above $7,000) and more than 29 million the overtime deduction (average above $3,100), mostly households under $100,000. Impact: Independent Tax Policy Center estimates put the average saving at about $1,480 for the roughly 3% of taxpayers who get the tips break and about $1,200 for the 10% who get the overtime break. Kept in part: real relief for those who qualify, but it is temporary, and the bill also cut Medicaid and SNAP.

stories.headline: Starshield slowdown for Ukraine came from White House, Reuters reports

stories.headline: Tesla Roadster flips and flies at reveal; production 2028
stories.body: In a show of less than 30 minutes near Waco, the new Roadster drove upside down on a suction system, lifted off and flipped in midair on SpaceX-built cold-gas thrusters, and jumped a truck. Musk set production for 2028 but gave no price. There are three trims: Performance (two seats, 0–60 under 1.6 seconds, $50,000 to reserve), Thrust (rear thrusters, under 0.9 seconds, $250,000 to reserve), and an invite-only, single-seat Rocket with a “full flight system” that isn’t street-legal. Tesla claims range over 300 miles (less than half the 620 promised in 2017) and top speed over 230 mph. Analysts see a low-volume halo car, and some read the event as marketing for a Tesla–SpaceX merger.

stories.headline: SpaceX seeks up to 456 Starship launches a year from Starbase
stories.body: The FAA has opened a full environmental review of SpaceX’s plan to raise Starbase, Texas, from 25 launches a year to as many as 456 launches and 912 landings, in two phases, starting with up to 100 launches. Public comments are open until Nov. 30, and no decision date is set. SpaceNews notes the FAA is also rewriting its launch rules to allow more launches overall. Context: Starship’s Flight 14 on Sept. 28 reached orbit and deployed its first Starlink V3 satellites.

stories.headline: Shuttle veteran Stephen Cash named Marshall Space Flight Center director
stories.body: Administrator Jared Isaacman named Stephen Cash director of Marshall in Huntsville, effective Monday, Oct. 19, calling him “a Marshall legend.” A four-decade veteran who once managed the shuttle propulsion program, Cash returns to the center where his career began; Rae Ann Meyer, who led the center during the transition, continues to serve. Marshall, with more than 5,000 civil-servant and contractor workers, runs the SLS rocket and the Human Landing System program and is central to NASA’s nuclear power and propulsion work.

stories.headline: No tax on tips and overtime: partly kept, capped through 2028
stories.body: Promise: Trump campaigned on ending federal taxes on tips and overtime. What was done: The July 2025 tax law created deductions, not a full repeal: up to $25,000 of tips, plus the extra “half” of time-and-a-half overtime, through 2028, with payroll taxes still owed. Treasury’s first-season data: more than 7.5 million filers claimed the tips deduction (average above $7,000) and more than 29 million the overtime deduction (average above $3,100), mostly households under $100,000. Impact: Independent Tax Policy Center estimates put the average saving at about $1,480 for the roughly 3% of taxpayers who get the tips break and about $1,200 for the 10% who get the overtime break. Kept in part: real relief for those who qualify, but it is temporary, and the bill also cut Medicaid and SNAP.

stories.headline: MAHA peptides plan reaches the White House, not yet in effect

Vatican City. Thursday afternoon’s medical update: routine checks were normal, the chest X-ray shows “good recovery of the lung that underwent surgery,” and Pope Leo XIV is doing his daily activities on his own with a full physiotherapy session. He concelebrated Mass again and has resumed work, meeting the Substitute of the Secretariat of State, Archbishop Paolo Rudelli, at Gemelli. Cardinal Parolin said the Nov. 6–17 South America trip will depend on what doctors say after discharge, and that the Pope may reshape parts of his pontificate later if needed; recovery is expected to take about a week in hospital.

Africa. Ethiopian forces and the allied Tigray Peace Force say they have entered Aksum; the monitor ACLED reports Eritrean troops pulling back across the border at Zalambessa, which Eritrea denies. Mauritius police say the island is calm and roads are clear after the week’s unrest.

Japan and the U.S. launched a roughly $21 billion chip-production project in New York state, and Japan’s foreign minister condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Europe. The EU summit ended its first day with no budget breakthrough; Sweden’s Kristersson said a deal may not come even by year’s end. Council President Costa takes over the talks, with a new proposal in a few weeks and a special summit Nov. 26.

North America. U.S. producer prices jumped the most in four and a half years in September, while retail sales beat forecasts; the 10-year Treasury yield had its biggest one-day drop in over a year, to about 5.06%. Tropical Storm Simon weakened to 50 mph off Mexico and should fade by the weekend, with no watches posted.

South America. Datafolha’s runoff poll also shows a tie: Flávio Bolsonaro 51%, Lula 49% of valid votes, within the margin of error, ten days before the Oct. 25 vote.

Oceania. Australia edged New Zealand 24–22 to open the Rugby League World Cup. Fiji’s cabinet endorsed a feasibility study for a roughly US$396 million ship-repair and shipbuilding yard at Lautoka, with Australian support for the next phase.

beats.title: World
beats.headline: Vatican City: Pope’s good second night; Yalu bridge opens; EU summit.
beats.body:
Vatican City. The Holy See Press Office said Thursday morning that Pope Leo XIV “had a good night in the hospital, got up and had breakfast”—his second night at Gemelli after Tuesday’s removal of the lower lobe of his right lung. Spokesman Matteo Bruni says the Pope wants to make the Nov. 6–17 Uruguay–Argentina–Peru trip; Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori said recovery could take weeks and the schedule might change, but the Holy See has announced no change. Today’s Bollettino: Father Ignatius Ding Zuyao was ordained bishop of Haimen, China, under the Holy See–China Provisional Agreement, and Bishop Paolo Andreolli, S.X., was named to Ponta de Pedras, Brazil (see Catholic). At the UN, Archbishop El Kassis told the First Committee that disarmament “cannot be postponed until more favourable circumstances arise.”

Africa. Secretary of State Rubio phoned Ethiopia’s Abiy Ahmed urging de-escalation with Eritrea under their 2018 peace deal, as Ethiopian forces expand control in northern Tigray. Kenya confirmed a second Ebola (Bundibugyo) case—a relative of the first patient who was already in quarantine; officials see no community spread. Mauritius extended its curfew through Friday morning after protests over water shortages and living costs; 94 arrests so far (16 minors), and schools are closed Thursday and Friday.

Asia. China and North Korea opened the New Yalu River Bridge Thursday morning—the four-lane, 3-km Dandong–Sinuiju crossing finished in 2014 but idle until now; Premier Li Qiang called it a “new landmark” of friendship. Singapore’s haze peaked at a season-high 24-hour PSI of 212 in the west at noon local time; masks are being distributed and 300+ community centers are serving as haze shelters. The EU–Gulf summit planned for Oct. 24 in Riyadh was postponed after repeated Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s airport.

Europe. EU leaders opened a two-day Brussels summit focused on energy prices (oil above $100, gas at its highest since winter 2022), a sharply divided 2028–34 budget, and Ukraine; draft conclusions lament the U.S. pause on Russian-diesel sanctions, which Bulgaria’s Radev backed as fuel-price relief while most leaders criticized it. Zelenskyy joins Friday. Radev also said he summoned Russia’s ambassador over the Black Sea drone strikes—logic points to Russia, he said, but there is no solid evidence yet; a full terror investigation starts when the ship damaged Tuesday reaches port.

North America. Simon is now a tropical storm (60 mph), nearly stationary about 270 miles south-southeast of Cabo San Lucas; it should drift northwest from Friday and fade by late weekend, with 1–3 inches of rain possible in Baja California Sur and no watches posted. Carney headlines a “Forever Canadian” rally in Calgary tonight ahead of Monday’s Alberta referendum. Panama reported its first death from the Oct. 9 magnitude-7.7 quake, and aftershocks are keeping hundreds from going home.

South America. Brazil’s first Quaest runoff poll has Flávio Bolsonaro 46%, Lula 44%—a statistical tie—ahead of the Oct. 25 vote; Datafolha publishes today. In Colombia, thousands marched peacefully Wednesday, led by ex-president Petro, against President Abelardo de la Espriella’s labor and pension proposals—the opposition’s first big show since he took office in August.

Oceania. Pacific Islands Forum chair Surangel Whipps of Palau, visiting Canberra, pushed back on critics counting absent leaders at last week’s Fiji–Tuvalu pre-COP and pressed for climate finance before COP31 opens Nov. 9; pledges to the Pacific Resilience Facility reached only half of a $500 million goal. Fiji approved a six-month, New Zealand–funded NZSIS review of its intelligence system amid foreign-interference concerns.

beats.title: MAGA / MAHA promises kept
beats.headline: Lower-prices pledge mostly unmet; ACA duplicate-subsidy sweep, some reinstated.
beats.body:
“Your groceries will be cheaper” — cost of living. Promise: Trump vowed cheaper groceries, gas under $2, 2% mortgages, and electricity bills cut in half. What was done: CBS News’s Oct. 14 tally finds food at home up 4% since November 2024, gas at $4.37 (up 47% since the Iran war began in late February), 30-year mortgages at 7.28%, and residential electricity up 12.5% since December 2024. The clear kept item: prescription-drug prices are down 3.9% since their February 2025 peak—the White House credits “most favored nation” pricing; experts also cite GLP-1 competition and more generics. Impact: With September CPI at 3.7%, nine in ten Americans tell CBS prices drive their view of the economy; the White House points to tax cuts, jobs, and trade deals.

“Crush fraud, waste, and abuse” — ACA subsidies. Promise: Kennedy and CMS’s Dr. Oz pledged to stop taxpayer money going where it shouldn’t. What was done: HHS said Oct. 14 it ended Obamacare subsidies this year for 189,000 enrollees who also had Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP or had died, projecting about $1.5 billion in savings over the next year, with a 30-day window to dispute. Impact: KFF Health News (via NPR) reports a separate sweep removed 760,000 enrollees and insurers say CMS has reinstated a small number wrongly cut; 419,000 more sign-ups are under review, with results due after the midterms. Supporters call the cleanup overdue; policy experts say there’s too little data to know how many legitimate members were caught.

People and the Moon. Vatican City. Afternoon medical bulletin: blood tests and a chest X-ray after Tuesday’s lobe removal were within expected ranges; Pope Leo XIV has begun respiratory physiotherapy, walked in his room, and resumed normal meals (breakfast and lunch). Holy See Press Office director Matteo Bruni later said the Pope concelebrated Mass Wednesday afternoon in a specially prepared 10th-floor room at Gemelli. Peru’s president floated that next month’s Latin America trip might need adjusting; the Holy See has not changed the Nov. 6–17 plan.

Africa. Quiet beyond this morning’s Ethiopia–Eritrea / Kabila / Ebola / Mauritius file. Mauritius police said traffic was moving again Wednesday morning after the overnight curfew, with cabinet reviewing next steps; no fresh Zalambessa or FRN headline after the morning wire.

Asia. Indonesia’s wildfire haze pushed Singapore’s 1-hour PM2.5 to about 284 µg/m³ in the west—the year’s high so far—and East Timor suspended in-person classes for three days from Oct. 15. China–North Korea’s New Yalu River Bridge still opens Thursday as planned.

beats.body:
Vatican City. The Holy See Press Office said early Wednesday that Pope Leo XIV “had a peaceful night” at Gemelli after Tuesday’s ~90-minute video-assisted removal of the lower lobe of his right lung, where adenocarcinoma was confirmed; more information is promised later today, and doctors are not yet discussing further therapy pending other test results. Cardinal Tagle, Dean of the College of Cardinals, presided this morning’s Amoris Laetitia tenth-anniversary closing Mass in St. Peter’s Square and read the Pope’s prepared homily on charity, chastity, and family prayer; the faithful prayed for “a serene convalescence.” The Bollettino also named Bishop Marek Forgáč archbishop of Košice (Slovakia) and Bishop Wellington de Queiroz Vieira archbishop of Cuiabá (Brazil). The Nov. 6–17 Uruguay–Argentina–Peru trip has not been changed.

Africa. Reuters-sourced reports say Ethiopian troops reached Zalambessa on the Eritrean border Tuesday as the UN Security Council met behind closed doors. In DR Congo, ex-president Joseph Kabila launched a new rebel coalition (FRN) in Goma with M23 leaders, while a UN envoy told the Council a peace “window” remains; Congo’s Ebola outbreak passed 9,000 confirmed cases. Mauritius imposed an overnight curfew over about a third of the island after unrest following a police shooting; 14 arrests reported.

Asia. China and North Korea open the long-delayed New Yalu River Bridge on Thursday, Xinhua says. Taiwan tracked 9 PLA aircraft (all crossing the median line), 6 navy and 6 official ships overnight. Taiwan confirmed plans to buy 6 million tons a year of Alaska LNG and possibly invest up to $4.4 billion.

Europe. Bulgaria says 11 crew remain missing from the sunk HS Dignity; PM Radev told parliament Russia has a motive but Sofia “cannot prove” it, and Bulgaria is seeking NATO/EU surveillance help. Ukraine and Moldova formally opened two more EU accession clusters (internal market; competitiveness). The Black Sea attacks head to the Oct. 15–16 European Council.

North America. Hurricane Simon, re-strengthened to Category 2 (about 105 mph), is drifting off Mexico’s Pacific coast and forecast to turn north toward Baja California Sur by the weekend; six dead from Simon and ex-Rachel. Alberta advance voting opened for Monday’s 10-question referendum, including separation; Carney rallies there Thursday–Friday. U.S. September CPI is due at 8:30 a.m. ET; forecasts see higher gasoline-driven headline inflation.

South America. Brazil’s electoral court warned the Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro campaigns over a record 162 censorship-style legal challenges since the first round; Band debate set for Oct. 18. Escondida supervisors reached a preliminary deal, putting off a strike pending a vote today. Argentina’s September inflation came in at 1.9%, a second month under 2%.

Oceania. Pacific nations told the UN its first sea-level-rise declaration falls short on statehood and maritime protections. Tuvalu defended last week’s Pre-COP and hailed Australia’s High Court coal-emissions ruling. More than 20 crews are fighting a wind-driven bushfire at Norwell on the northern Gold Coast.

beats.title: MAGA / MAHA promises kept
beats.headline: Alaska LNG pledge firms up; bird-flu vaccine plan stalled.
beats.body:
“Unleash American energy” — Alaska LNG. Promise: Trump pledged to get the long-stalled North Slope gas line built. What was done: At Tuesday’s Wasilla rally he and Commerce Secretary Lutnick said Taiwan will buy 30% of the project’s gas for 20 years and invest $4.4 billion; Taiwan’s economy ministry confirmed plans to buy 6 million tons a year. Impact: A real step for the buyer side, but Alaska’s gasline agency says Taiwan’s 30% offtake is still non-binding with price and term “nearing conclusion,” South Korea has not confirmed the $50 billion Trump cites, and no construction start has been announced—so no change yet in Alaskans’ energy bills.

“Cheaper eggs” meets MAHA vaccine skepticism — bird flu. Promise: Trump campaigned on egg prices; Kennedy on questioning vaccines. What was done: Politico reports (five sources) that USDA shelved a poultry-vaccination strategy in 2025, with Kennedy’s views a major factor. Impact: Biosecurity steps alone have not stopped spread (about 2 million birds hit in the last three months); Republican senators and egg producers warn migration season could push protein prices back up.

beats.title: World
beats.headline: Vatican City: Pope surgery OK; Bulgaria missing; Brazil polls.
beats.body:
Vatican City. Doctors at Gemelli successfully removed the lower lobe of Pope Leo XIV’s right lung in a ~90-minute video-assisted operation Tuesday afternoon; intraoperative histology confirmed lung adenocarcinoma as preoperative tests had suggested. No complications; he awoke normally, returned to the 10th-floor room, asked for dinner, and spent the evening with secretaries and Vatican staff. About one week in hospital still expected; audiences remain canceled through Oct. 20. Wednesday morning update planned on how he spent the night.

Africa. The U.S.-requested UN Security Council held closed Horn of Africa consultations Tuesday on Ethiopia–Eritrea escalation after Ethiopian forces entered Adwa; no public resolution or Council statement followed the session.

Asia. Quiet beyond this morning’s Seoul–Washington–Tokyo consults and KCNA’s “big success” claim on Monday’s tactical ballistic test; Taiwan’s overnight PLA track (five aircraft, six PLAN ships) still the latest island watch.

Europe. After this morning’s Black Sea drone hits, Bulgaria said the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3 (15 crew rescued, six injured) was struck by three drones; the second ship sank with search ongoing for missing crew. Sofia summoned Russia’s ambassador and said it would deploy more unmanned maritime/air surveillance; PM sought NATO and EU support.

North America. Hurricane Simon remained a small Category 1 west of Cabo Corrientes; mainland Mexico watches were discontinued while rain and swell risk lingered for Baja and the Pacific coast. Combined flood/landslide deaths tied to Simon and former Rachel rose to at least six.

South America. Fresh runoff polls toward Oct. 25 put Flávio Bolsonaro narrowly ahead of Lula within margins of error (Datafolha ~49–45 raw; other houses near a technical tie on valid votes).

Oceania. Queensland’s Valentine Plains fire near Biloela stayed on the evening watch; South Australia’s Strathalbyn bushfire emergency was downgraded with residents still urged to monitor conditions.
